lawyer:
S. R. Pal with S. C. Das ------ For the Petitioner.  

K. Z. Alam, D.A.G. Mahmudul Islam  ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
M/s. Khan Bros. Ltd  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, J.—This writ petition is at the instance of M/s. Khan Brothers Ltd. a private limited company and raises a short but important question of law in that the properties held by a company registered within the territories now comprising Bangladesh during Pakistan regime, could be said to be abandoned property, in terms of section 2 of Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972 (hereinafter referred to as Abandoned Property Order). To appreciate these point facts as emerge from the affidavits of the parties may be set out. Khan Brothers Ltd. is a private limited Company with seven share-holders, divided into five thousand shares as on 28.2.72 the day Presidential Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated. Of the seven share-holders, lion's share was held by Khan. A. Sabur and he were the life Managing Director holding 2369 shares. Among the other six share-holders, one M. A. Samad who held 200 shares, has been admitted to be a Pakistani, and was not resident in Bangladesh at that time. The other five members of the Company have been asserted to be the nationals of Bangladesh and resident in Bangladesh. The Company had a Board of Directors consisting of four members including the Life Managing Director. They are Q. A. Rashid, Mrs. N. R. Khanam and Rouf Khan. After the creation of Bangladesh on the surrender of the Pakistani occupation Army, on the 16th of December, 1971, on 31st of January, 1972 Q. A. Rashid was appointed Director-in-charge of the Company. On 22nd February, 1972 Khan A. Sabur against whom charge of collaboration under the Collaborator's Order, 1972 was hanging, surrendered before the S. D. O. (s) at Dhaka. In his absence the Company was run by the Director-in-charge and the Board of Directors. Upon some instruction from the Government, the Additional Deputy 'Commissioner of Khulna on 29.8. 72, took over the management of the assets of the Company which consisted of a jute godown and jute bailing press at Daulatpur, Khulna. On 1.9.72 a representation was made by Q.A. Rashid the Director-in-charge to the Government for the release of the properties asserting, that they are not 'abandoned property'. But on that date a Gazette Notification was issued by the Government in the following terms: 

 "No. Ind. M-XVI-9(12)172/199(5)—1st September 1972 In exercise of the authority given by the Articles 4 and 5 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) and the rules made thereunder, the Ministry of Industries is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders the management of M/s. Khan Brothers Ltd., Daulatpur, Khulna, including all its properties and assets whenever located in Bangladesh and to put it under the Management Board Group-A-Khulna Area. The Management Board shall operate this unit and generally conduct all its affairs including operation of Bank accounts. 

 This Notification is under challenge, and has given rise to the question of law set out above. On 6th December, 1973, Khan A. Sabur was released following a general amnesty granted by the Government. He then started making various representations, the last one being on 12.6.74, but none received any favorable reply. Thereafter the petitioner-company moved this Court, and obtained this Rule. It is resisted by the Government asserting the validity of the impugned notification, on the ground that the properties in question ate abandoned property in terms of the Presidential Order No. 16 of 1972. 

 2. We turn the point set out above. According to the Government the properties of the Company are an abandoned property in terms of the 'Abandoned Property Order'. The petitioner says that the properties do not come within the mischief of the Order. The main controversy, therefore, center’s round the interpretation of the word 'Abandoned Property' as set out in the President's Order. There are some other subsidiary points and they will be dealt with presently. 

 3. From the facts set out above we get that the Company was registered in the territory now comprising Bangladesh, and on the relevant date namely 28.2.72 when the Abandoned Property Order came into operation, it was being run by a Board of Directors of the Company, as in the meantime the Life Managing Director had surrendered to the Government under the  Collaborator's Order. According to the Government, this management was done by unauthorised persons, without clearly articulating as to who were the unauthorised occupants or how, if at all, was the company run. The petitioner has unequivocally asserted that after the surrender of their Life Managing Director, the Company was run by the Board of Directors and Q. A. Rashid as the Director-in-charge. The report of the Deputy Commissioner Annexure "B" proceeds on the basis that some of the original share-holders were non-Muslims, and that the company was managed by unauthorized persons. But nothing has been elucidated or clarified as to who were the persons in unauthorized management or occupation of the properties of the Company.—There is no clear denial to the assertion of the petitioner, that it is the Board of Directors who were managing the Company and Q. A. Rashid was the Director-in-charge, Therefore on fact, we held that it was the Board of Directors of the Company who at the relevant time when running the Company. The properties of the company cannot be said to be unoccupied. 

 4. Let us now turn to the question of law. Conceding for the moment that the property was run by unauthorised persons, could it then be said to be an Abandoned Property. This brings us to deal with the definition of "Abandoned Property" as set out in the Abandoned Property Order. It is found in Article 2 of the said President's Order and may be set out in full: 

 (1) 'abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including— 

 (i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971 was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 

 (ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972) but does not include—(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. 

 (b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 

 "Before dealing with the contention of Mr. K. Z. Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government, let us deal with the question as we find from the reading of the Article. The definition given is not a very clear language. The legislative authority has tried first to define 'abandoned property', then gave it an inclusive meaning, and then again excluded certain categories of properties. We will deal with the definition portion presently. Let us first refer to those properties which have been included and those excluded. Of the included properties are : (1) properties owned by any person who is a citizen of the State at war with the People's Republic of Bangladesh at any time after 25th day of March, 1971 which in short means West Pakistan, now Pakistan; (2) any property taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1/72. 

 5. The excluded properties are: (1) any property whose owner is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; (2) any property which is in possession of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 

 6. Keeping in view the inclusive definition and exclusion, let us approach the controversial definition clause which is clans; (1). It consists of three clauses one principal clause, and two subordinate clauses. The principal clause says that abandoned property means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh. This principal clause is followed by two subordinate clauses each of which begins with a relative pronoun 'whose' or 'who'. The first clause says "whose whereabouts are not known" and the second says, 'who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property'. In our opinion the legislative authority while defining 'abandoned property' has used a complex sentence containing a principal clause, and two subordinate clauses. The two subordinate clauses are dependent on the principal clause, though they themselves are disjunctive. The principal clause denotes persons, and the subordinate clauses connote the contentions under which property of the denoted persons will become abandoned property. An explanation has been appended saying, "person who is not present in Bangladesh is to include any body of persons, or a company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of the State which was at war with the People's Republic of Bangladesh at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971." The explanation in our opinion gives a clue to the interpretation we are trying to give to the definition clause contained in sub-article (1). The legislative authority has gone on the basis of clauses, and not on the basis of words taken separately. The legislative authority has taken whole clause viz. the principal clause of sub-article (1) to for explanation. Giving its grammatical meaning, we find that 'abandoned property' will be that property whose owner, either natural or artificial person like corporation, is not present in Bangladesh. That is the first precondition, but not the whole inasmuch as the principal clause is qualified by two subordinate but alternative clauses. The first precondition of absence from Bangladesh must be added with any of the two attributes contained in the alternative subordinate clauses. The other precondition is alternative; one is whose whereabouts are not known, and the other, who has ceased to occupy or manage or supervise this property. And when both the preconditions of the principal and subordinate clauses though alternative, are present, then the property will bear answer to the definition of abandoned property. The last phrase 'manage in person' in our opinion means in case of natural person by himself, and in the case of artificial person, one who in terms of its rules of constitution is authorised to manage. We therefore find that abandoned property, will be that property whose owner is not present in Bangladesh and whose where about are either is not known, or who has ceased to occupy,' supervise or manage in person his property. 

 7. If we again turn to the principal clause, we find, that the Words 'Who is not present' requires some interpretation. The wards is our opinion mean who is voluntarily not present. It does not and cannot mean who is compelled or unable to be present; in other words when the person of his own volition, or free will is not present, but not against his volition or will. We think the conditions set out for the exclusion of property give some indication, on the construction of the sub-article. The interpretation completely harmonies the meaning of all the sub-articles. It is equally in accord with in the preamble of the Order which says that it is expedient to make provisions for the control, management and disposal of certain property abandoned by certain persons who are not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who have ceased to occupy or supervise or manage in person their property, or who are enemy aliens. Construed thus, we find that the definition clauses affirmatively means, whose owner is not present in Bangladesh and whose whereabouts is either not known or who has ceased to manage, supervise or occupy the property; negatively, we get abandoned property does not comprehend property whose owner is a Bengalee resident in Bangladesh, albeit, the person may be natural or artificial, like Company. 

 8. So far as company is concerned its domicile is governed by the country of its incorporation. We have found that the registered office of the petitioner company is Bangladesh, and so it is a Bangali Company. We have also held that its properties and assets were run and managed by its Board of Directors. Therefore any property held by the petitioner-company domiciled in Bangladesh, is outside the ambit of the definition of abandoned property, and they are immune from the operation of the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order. The impugned notification therefore was issued without lawful authority. 

 10. Mr. Alam's submission may be tested in another way, if we take the second exclusion. We find, it has clearly provided, that all properties whose management have been taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 though could be treated as abandoned property, yet shall not include those properties whose owner is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose, which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The exclusion is clear and significant. This distinction emphasises the point we have indicated. Not the properties of all persons living outside Bangladesh are abandoned properties, if the Government is of opinion that their stay abroad is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. We find no authority to the wide proposition of the learned Deputy Attorney-General to hold that mere non-occupation of a property by any owner resident or not in Bangladesh, will make the property abandoned. We find no merit in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General. 

 11. There is a question of Samad's holding 200 shares in the Company and no doubt Samad is a Pakistani as the petitioner in its representation to the Government has admitted him to be so. In terms of Article 8, his shares are abandoned properties. The Government under sub-article 1(b) could purchase the other shares of the Company, but has not proceeded to do so. And so neither the management of the property nor assets of the company vest in the Government nor can the Government claim to do so. 

 12. For the reasons we make the Rat absolute, and declare that the Notification No. Ind. M-XVI-9(12)/72/199(5) dated 1st September, 1972 issued by the Ministry of Industries Division published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary Wednesday, September 6, 1972 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and the Respondents are directed to hand over the possession of the property taken over by the impugned Notification to the petitioner-company. We however, make no order as to costs.
